"title": "Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement",
"authors": "Takahiro Nakahara (Osaka Metropolitan University); Takashi Kobayashi (Chuo University); Tetsuji Dohi (Chuo University); Takeshi Yoshimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Norifumi Fujimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Daisuke Kiriya (Osaka Metropolitan University)",
"field_subfield": "2D materials / optoelectronics (photoluminescence engineering of monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides)",
"type_of_paper": "Experimental study (materials science / condensed matter physics)",
"executive_summary": "Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) of the form MX 2 (M = Mo, W and X = S, Se) are attractive for thin, mechanically robust crystals with a three-atom layer thickness and a direct band gap at the K and Kʹ points, making them promising for optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. However, their poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity—caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline-lattice defects—limits their optical behavior. For sulfur-based compounds such as MoS 2 and WS 2 , PL enhancement has been largely established by chemical treatments including p-type dopants such as 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8-tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) and tetrafluoro-1,4-benzoquinone, and by superacid molecules such as bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI), which can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times. These methods decrease the probability of generating trions and enhance exciton-dominated emission, but they are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe 2 and WSe 2 , where only oleic acid and hydrohalic acid treatments or defect repairing have shown limited success. The authors of this study developed a universal postpreparation method that removes the substrate effect by coating monolayer TMDCs with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, which has a melting point of 42-45 °C. Because of the large thermal coefficient of paraffin, the stain is effectively applied to the TMDCs in the coating process, and the paraffin-coated monolayers show spontaneous fluctuation that, in an extreme case, forms the shape of a bundle. During this fluctuation and deformation, the substrate effect is removed, and PL intensity improves remarkably in both sulfur- and selenium-based compounds. For example, MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 show factors of enhancement of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold from the as-exfoliated flakes, respectively, and a monolayer WS 2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times through paraffin coating. The mechanism is attributed to a combination of strain induced by the volume change caused by the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin and the subsequent desorption of the monolayer flakes from the substrate, which is confirmed by Raman shifts of the Eʹ peak by about -0.72 cm -1 and the Aʹ peak by 1.03 cm -1 in 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 . This universal strategy extends the design of applying TMDCs as optoelectronic materials due to the transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility of the paraffin, and it is applicable to other 2D layered materials.",

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara (Osaka Metropolitan University); Takashi Kobayashi (Chuo University); Tetsuji Dohi (Chuo University); Takeshi Yoshimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Norifumi Fujimura (Osaka Metropolitan University); Daisuke Kiriya (Osaka Metropolitan University)

summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study (materials science / condensed matter physics)
summary.executive_summary: Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) of the form MX 2 (M = Mo, W and X = S, Se) are attractive for thin, mechanically robust crystals with a three-atom layer thickness and a direct band gap at the K and Kʹ points, making them promising for optical transistors, light-emitting diodes, and solar cells. However, their poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity—caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and crystalline-lattice defects—limits their optical behavior. For sulfur-based compounds such as MoS 2 and WS 2 , PL enhancement has been largely established by chemical treatments including p-type dopants such as 2,3,5,6-tetrafluoro-7,7,8,8-tetracyanoquinodimethane (F4TCNQ) and tetrafluoro-1,4-benzoquinone, and by superacid molecules such as bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI), which can produce PL enhancement of hundreds of times. These methods decrease the probability of generating trions and enhance exciton-dominated emission, but they are not effective for the selenium-based TMDCs of MoSe 2 and WSe 2 , where only oleic acid and hydrohalic acid treatments or defect repairing have shown limited success. The authors of this study developed a universal postpreparation method that removes the substrate effect by coating monolayer TMDCs with a simple hydrocarbon, paraffin, which has a melting point of 42-45 °C. Because of the large thermal coefficient of paraffin, the stain is effectively applied to the TMDCs in the coating process, and the paraffin-coated monolayers show spontaneous fluctuation that, in an extreme case, forms the shape of a bundle. During this fluctuation and deformation, the substrate effect is removed, and PL intensity improves remarkably in both sulfur- and selenium-based compounds. For example, MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 show factors of enhancement of 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold from the as-exfoliated flakes, respectively, and a monolayer WS 2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times through paraffin coating. The mechanism is attributed to a combination of strain induced by the volume change caused by the high thermal expansion coefficient of the paraffin and the subsequent desorption of the monolayer flakes from the substrate, which is confirmed by Raman shifts of the Eʹ peak by about -0.72 cm -1 and the Aʹ peak by 1.03 cm -1 in 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 . This universal strategy extends the design of applying TMDCs as optoelectronic materials due to the transparency, flexibility, and biocompatibility of the paraffin, and it is applicable to other 2D layered materials.

claims.description: Paraffin coating provides a universal strategy for enhancing PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs.
The PL enhancement is due to a combination of strain and desorption of the monolayer from the substrate.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs are attractive for their thin, mechanically robust crystals with a direct band gap. Their poor PL intensity is a major drawback limiting optical applications. Sulfur-based compounds have established PL enhancement via chemical treatments. Selenium-based compounds lack effective PL enhancement strategies. No universal strategy exists for improving optical behavior across diverse 2D semiconductors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a universal method can enhance PL across sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs. The hypothesis is that paraffin coating removes the substrate effect and enhances PL universally. The predicted outcome is that spontaneous fluctuation and desorption remove the substrate effect. The predicted mechanism involves strain from paraffin's high thermal expansion coefficient. The predicted result is large PL enhancement factors across all four compounds.

Methodological Details
The paraffin used has a melting point of 42-45 °C. The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C before coating. A spin coater was used to apply the paraffin coating. A heat blower was applied to keep the paraffin melted during spin coating. The prepared film is transparent, enabling optical observation and PL measurement. PL enhancement was observed on both Si/SiO 2 and quartz substrates. Raman analysis was performed on 30 samples of monolayer MoS 2 . The Eʹ peak represents in-plane vibrations sensitive to strain. The Aʹ peak represents out-of-plane vibrations sensitive to carrier concentration. The number of tested compounds and their enhancement factors are reported. The sample was surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides to prevent bundling. The sample was examined at room temperature over time.

Procedures And Architectures
The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C before being dropped onto the sample. A heat blower was used to keep the paraffin in a melted state during spin coating. The paraffin covers the entire monolayer, confirmed by optical microscopy. PL mapping confirmed enhancement across the whole plane with partial greater enhancement. A thick film of paraffin by simple casting resulted in a nontransparent glassy appearance. The paraffin coating was applied to all four monolayer TMDCs. The factor of enhancement was dependent on each sample. The Eʹ peak shifted negatively by about -0.72 cm -1 after paraffin coating. The Aʹ peak shifted positively by 1.03 cm -1 after paraffin coating. The PL intensity in the center was about 2.3 times greater than at the rim. The PL peak position around the center shifted 5-10 meV lower in energy than the rim. The deformation into a bundle occurs in an extreme case.

MoS 2 showed a remarkable PL enhancement factor of 215 due to its low as-exfoliated signal. The PL enhancement factors were 215-, 55-, 9-, and 50-fold for MoS 2 , WS 2 , WSe 2 , and MoSe 2 . A monolayer WS 2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times through paraffin coating. The normalized PL spectrum showed a decrease in the trion-derived shoulder.
